newsitem.title: UK: UK sugar beets progressing well, crop diseases low.
newsitem.headline: UK sugar beets progressing well, crop diseases low.

text.p: Britain's 1997/98 sugar beet crop looks to have conquered its initial setbacks and has a low incidence of field pests, beet experts said on Friday.
The crop has also enjoyed much-needed rains in the past two weeks, evening up beet establishment and correcting earlier patchy emergence.
"The crop has been growing a lot with the rain. I think at the moment the crop is holding its own," said an official at independent consultants ADAS.
Dry spells and frost affected this year's beets at the critical germination stage, partially offsetting the advantage gained after planting was completed ahead of last year's programme.
Industry sources said fields were generally free of pest and disease.
Last week beet growers received a warning of downy mildew but experts said this week's cooler weather seemed to have prevented a further recurrence. Incidence was reported to be low at one percent.
"There's been very healthy growing with the rain," said an official at the National Farmers Union (NFU).
"There's very little disease about but there have been outbreaks of things like downy mildew which are unusual but I don't think are causing too much concern."

In a recent bulletin, the industry-funded IACR-Broom's Barn research centre said numbers of aphids -- which lead to the virus yellows disease -- were still low on treated and untreated fields although some were starting to be found in Essex, east of London.

Aphids would probably find leaves of early drilled crops unpalatable and the effect of virus yellows after the 20-leaf stage was negligible. Any aphids coming into such fields were unlikely to warrant chemical spraying, it said.

But if warmer weather were to arrive next week ahpid numbers could still increase, particularly in the crops which were sown later. Rain is expected to continue into early next week with temperatures below normal for the time of year.
"Aphids generally on beets, potatoes and cereals are low but they are ubiquitous and could increase almost anywhere," the ADAS official said.
Leaf miners, caterpillars and flea beetles did not appear to be major problems at present, the Broom's Barn report said.
While pygmy beetles could be found in a few crops, beets were growing fast so that they could keep up a sustained attack on the crop, it added.
Some weeds are already showing above beet plants but this was not expected to be too much of a problem for growers, although it would cost them more.

"It's going to have been an expensive year (for growers) with the way things have gone," the NFU official said. "The early lack of rain and the weed control element is going to mean more expense with more numbers of runs over the crop to deal with weeds."
